In Support of Leonhard; Your Thoughts?
stories.summary:
I personally believe in Coach Leonhard and his coaching staff's ability to solve the secondary problem. I saw this posted a couple of days ago but I can't remember where. These are his exact words, giving credit to his handle. What do you defense-minded posters think of it?



	 



	Bills defense observation by @yourwrong6861:



	The "basics" of coverage are not the issue. The issue is getting enough repetition as a secondary unit for pattern matching and match zone coverages, which is the staple of Leonhard's D.



	If I were Buffalo, I would go trade for Rasul Douglas...tomorrow. He is well experienced with the concepts Leonhard runs...and would be THE perfect mentor for IGB (and Benford for that matter) in these concepts. I think Max will rarely see the field the rest of the season, unless it's dime.



	Another thing the local media got wrong, was throwing their hands in the air, wondering "why" Buffalo would move up to draft IGB. IGB was one of the best CB prospects that fit Leonhard's coverage concepts. He wasn't drafted to play situational "press man". He was drafted to eventually be a starter. He's light years better than Hairston in Leonhard's coverage concepts.



	Yet another thing everyone got wrong? The thought that Leonhard's scheme was based on "press man". His bread and butter is man coverage through these zone concepts in the form of match zone...not press.



	It's ridiculous we have gone 5 games and no local media talks about this. It's created this false narrative that the secondary sucks...the LBers suck.



	Historically, it takes 8-10 games for a coverage unit to have Leonhard's concepts become second nature.  And the local media has a fanbase falsely screaming for every player's head on the defense, excluding the DL.

Sabres come back again, but fall to Canadiens in overtime
stories.summary:
Buffalo erases another two-goal deficit, but Cole Caufield ends the night just 54 seconds into overtime



Boxscore



Score: Buffalo Sabres 3-4 Montreal Canadiens (OT)



Shots: BUF 26-34 MTL



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Norris 2 (Helenius), Quinn (Benson, Samuelsson) SHG, Thompson (Doan, Kulich)



Montreal Canadiens Goals: Bolduc (Suzuki, Slafkovsky) PPG, Caufield (Slafkovsky, Carrier), Texier (Guhle, Carrier), Caufield (Unassisted) OT



Goaltending: Luukkonen 30 saves (.882 SV%), Fowler 23 saves (.885 SV%)



Additional Stats: Buffalo won 36.8% of faceoffs, recorded 18 hits and blocked 17 shots.



Quick Thoughts



First Period – A Good Start Doesn’t Last



For once, the Buffalo Sabres didn’t have to spend the opening minutes digging themselves out of a hole. Josh Norris got Buffalo on the board first, taking a feed from Konsta Helenius and beating Jacob Fowler at 8:21 to give the Sabres a 1-0 lead. Unfortunately, that lead didn’t last long. Montreal answered just over three minutes later when Zachary Bolduc scored on the power play. Cole Caufield followed with another goal at 14:01, and Buffalo suddenly trailed 2-1 after the opening period. It has become a familiar problem for the Sabres this season. Even when they start well, they have struggled to control games and keep opponents from building momentum. Buffalo has shown it can battle back when things aren’t going its way, but it would be nice to see them play with a lead for a change.



Second Period – Jack Quinn to the Rescue



Buffalo got worse early in the second period. Alexandre Texier scored at 7:39, extending Montreal’s lead to 3-1 and putting the Sabres in another two-goal hole. Sound familiar? Just two nights earlier, the Sabres trailed Toronto 4-2 entering the third period before rallying for an overtime win. Apparently, Buffalo tried the same approach against Montreal. Jack Quinn, who was outstanding against Toronto, continued his strong play by scoring a shorthanded goal at 9:52 of the second period. With assists from Zach Benson and Mattias Samuelsson, Quinn brought Buffalo back within one and gave the Sabres some much-needed life. Quinn has quickly become one of Buffalo’s most important offensive contributors. His chemistry with Benson has grown exponentially, and if he keeps this up, he will earn a nice payday. Whether it’s scoring, creating opportunities, or sparking the offense when the team desperately needs it, he keeps finding ways to make an impact. He even made a great backcheck to split up a two-on-one.



Third Period – Here We Go Again



At this point, the Buffalo Sabres might actually prefer playing from behind. For the third straight game, Buffalo needed a comeback, and the Sabres delivered again. This time, Tage Thompson stepped up. At 10:12 of the third period, Thompson finished a play set up by Josh Doan and Jiri Kulich, beating Fowler to tie the game at three. Just like that, another two-goal deficit had disappeared. The Sabres had erased a 3-1 deficit against Montreal on Tuesday, came back from 4-2 down against Toronto on Thursday, and now had fought back from another 3-1 hole against the Canadiens. There is certainly something to be said about a team that refuses to quit. The Sabres have shown impressive resilience early this season, particularly in the third period. When they turn up the offensive pressure and start moving the puck with confidence, they can make life difficult for opponents. But this has become an almost ridiculous trend. Why does Buffalo need to be trailing by two goals before it starts playing its best hockey? The tying goal ensured the Sabres would collect at least one point, but another overtime appearance was waiting.



Overtime – That Didn’t Take Long



After needing overtime against Montreal on Tuesday and Toronto on Thursday, the Sabres were headed back to three-on-three hockey for the third straight game. Unfortunately, this overtime period didn’t last very long. Just 54 seconds into the extra frame, Cole Caufield scored his second goal of the night to give Montreal the 4-3 victory. And just like that, another dramatic Buffalo comeback ended with only one point to show for it. The Sabres have now played beyond regulation four times in their first nine games, including three consecutive overtime or shootout appearances. Buffalo might be getting comfortable playing extra hockey, but there is a difference between fighting back to earn a point and finishing the job.



At The Horn



The Buffalo Sabres are becoming one of the NHL’s most entertaining and frustrating teams to watch. On one hand, this team has shown it can overcome adversity. They don’t seem rattled when trailing by multiple goals, and their offensive players have consistently stepped up when needed. On the other hand, the Sabres are making things unnecessarily difficult for themselves. 



Montreal outshot Buffalo 34-26 and dominated in the faceoff circle, winning 63.2% of the draws. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made 30 saves to keep Buffalo within striking distance, but the Sabres once again struggled to play a complete game. 



There are certainly positives to take away from the night. Quinn continued his offensive production, Thompson delivered another important goal, and Norris got Buffalo off to a promising start. But the larger issue remains. The Sabres have now erased two-goal deficits in three straight games. That speaks to their character, but it also raises serious questions about their ability to dictate games rather than constantly reacting to what their opponents do. 



Last season’s successful team found ways to win games without needing dramatic third-period comebacks every night. Buffalo needs to find that same consistency. It’s encouraging to know the Sabres can come back from almost anything. It’s considerably less encouraging that they keep putting themselves in those situations. With a 4-3-2 record in nine games, Buffalo has earned valuable points despite inconsistent performances. But overtime-loser points won’t be enough if the Sabres want to establish themselves as a legitimate contender in the Atlantic Division, and any point earned without Dahlin in the lineup is a good one.

stories.summary:
It’s Déjà Vu All Over Again With Buffalo Back at Bell Centre



Buffalo Sabres (4-3-1) vs Montreal Canadiens (3-3-1)

*knock knock* “Who’s there?” “It’s Déjà Vu”



“Déjà Vu who?”



*knock knock*



What to Watch



1. Do Not Adjust Your TV Sets



The Sabres once again return to the friendly confinds of Bell Centre in Montreal tonight with just four days and one game in Toronto between visits. Unusual scheduling to be sure. This second go-around will finish off the Maple Leaf sandwich with another slice of Montreal French bread.



Last time out, Buffalo stormed back to steal a point in the standings before imploding in the shootout. The Sabres will need a better, more consistent effort in tonight’s matchup with the Habs to come out a winner. No more two-shot periods allowed!



The bad news for Buffalo is that Rasmus Dahlin has been ruled out again for today’s game against the Canadiens, Matthew Fairburn of The Athletic reports.



Head coach Lindy Ruff said Thursday that Dahlin was 50/50 to play Saturday, but the 26-year-old won’t travel with the team to Montreal after all. However, Ruff said Friday that Dahlin is progressing, so it seems possible that he’ll be a candidate to return Wednesday against the Flyers. He remains listed as day-to-day for now.



2. Four Jacks



Jack Quinn tied his career-best performance as a pro in Buffalo’s thrilling 5-4 overtime win over Toronto on Thursday night. The talented winger recorded two goals and two assists for a satisfying four-point night. He also showed some toughness after being confronted by Toronto’s Troy Stecher, handling himself well in a brief fight. To cap off the evening, Quinn set up Owen Power for the overtime winner. What a hand he played for the comeback victory.



Quinn has looked noticeably more confident and effective on the ice this season, as things finally appear to be coming together for the fifth-year Sabre. He is tied for the team lead in both goals and points while averaging 19:20 of ice time per game. Lindy Ruff has repeatedly praised Quinn’s improved speed, growing confidence, and playmaking ability as he enters a crucial contract year. Along with Noah Östlund and Zach Benson, Quinn has helped form what has arguably been Buffalo’s best forward line this season.



Jack has been a major factor so far this year for Buffalo and Thursday’s performance was another encouraging sign of his development. The Sabres will need him to keep this momentum going if the team hopes to build on its recent success. If Quinn continues to play with this level of confidence and consistency, he could be in for a breakout season at just the right time.








Photo Credit: Buffalo Sabres




3. Concussion Grenade



Off to a slow start with just two points in eight games, Josh Norris now finds himself in concussion protocol. At this point, it almost feels like the Sabres’ injury report isn’t complete without him.



Norris collided awkwardly with Oliver Ekman-Larsson during overtime in Toronto and did not return to finish the game. He’s listed as day-to-day and will likely miss at least a game or two. 



UPDATE Norris surprisingly practiced on Friday but the return-to-play process typically spans a minimum of 5 to 6 days (though actual return depends on symptom resolution).



Tyson Kozak can’t step into Norris’s spot as he has been sent home, but Jiri Kulich is the likely option if he’s feeling better. Kulich was recently sent back to Buffalo himself to be evaluated over concerns related to the blood clot he suffered last season. Fortunately, he checked out fine. Jiri has since returned to the team and is listed as a possibility to play tonight.



It’s been a disappointing start to the season for Norris. He opened the year playing top-line minutes but struggled to generate much offense. More recently, he’s been shuffled around the lineup and has seen mostly bottom-six duty. Now he’s dealing with another injury, although this one hopefully won’t keep him out for long. The Sabres are starting to get a little thin at forward.



With Norris, though, you can never be too comfortable. He could get injured opening his mail. 



SECOND UPDATE Norris practiced again this morning and is now a possibility to play tonight. I have to wonder how that’s possible, given the NHL’s mandates with concussions. Either his new evaluation determined he wasn’t actually suffering from a concussion, or something has changed rather quickly.

stories.title: Overtime Strategy: Kick or Receive?
stories.summary:
The Rams won the toss and elected to kick to the Bills, which seems to be the prevailing wisdom, with the thinking that after the receiving team's possession, the kicking team gets the ball back, knowing what they need to either win or tie the game.  Most teams who win the OT coin toss seem to be electing to kick.  I disagree with this strategy, especially in the regular season, where the OT period is limited to 10 minutes.



	 



	First, the receiving team can chew up the clock, maybe as much as seven or eight minutes.  If they score a TD, then the kicking team might have as little as 2:30 left by the time they get the ball, which limits the type of drive they can mount, especially if they've already used one of their two OT timeouts.  More importantly, if the receiving team doesn't score, then punts the ball to the kicking team, they know that if they get a stop, they will get the ball next with a chance to win the game with a FG.  So in essence, they have a good chance to get two possessions, while the kicking team is probably only going to get one, unless both teams go three-and-out quickly.  I think the opportunity to get an "extra" possession outweighs the advantage the kicking team gets from knowing what they need. 



	 



	And here's another point.  With the new kickoff rule, the receiving team is likely to get the ball at their own 35-yardline or better.  If they advance it even to their own 40, they can pin the kicking team deep in their own territory with a punt, significantly reducing the kicking team's chance of scoring.  That is exactly what happened to the Bills in the playoff game against Denver.  Even though their defense got a stop on Denver's first possession, the Bills started their only OT possession inside their own 10-yard line. To me, if we have a choice in OT, we should always elect to receive. 



	 



	Thoughts?

stories.title: The Rise and Fall of the Bills Defense
stories.summary:
Here are our defensive ranks over the past ten years:



	 



	



	 
	
		 
	



	McD turned the D around and achieved a Top 6 finish four times in five years from 2018 to 2022.  



	 



	In 2017, our D was putrid and was ranked 26th.  So far this season we're putrid again and ranked 30th.  In between these ugly bookends, we averaged 7th.   



	 



	Milano and some other key players were hurt in 2020 when the D was middle-of-the-pack.  In fact, injuries to key defensive players have been a common theme over the past several years.  On offense, Josh has never missed a game and he is our offense.  But on D, it seems we suffer more than our fair share from key defender injuries.  This trend has certainly hurt us in the playoffs.  



	 



	During McD's glory years on defense, the best players were Milano, Poyer, Hyde, and White.  These were all Whaley guys.  As they aged out, our rankings dropped.  Beane has struggled to find equivalently talented playmakers on D.   



	 



	Lezlie Frazier was our DC during the Bills' best defensive years (2018-2022), which may or may not be coincidental.



	 



	I'd love to hear from @GunnerBill and other smart talent evaluators about how personnel affected our rise and fall.  Or @HoofHearted and other smart X-and-O guys about how scheme has impacted these rankings.  



	 



	As a Bills fan, I live in a constant state of hope.  I hope Leonhard figures things out and fields a capable defense by the end of the regular season.  One that helps us win our first Lombardi.  But I'd be lying if I didn't say I have concerns about Leonhard's D, as early as it is in the season.

What was that first period? Minus Jiri Kulich the entire team except one Jack Quinn seemed to be absent and anything the Leafs got came from Buffalo errors. 




Jack Quinn is the beneficiary of a Toronto turnover after Zach Benson pressured Blankenburg, 1-1 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/xKuELj0Cl0— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 15, 2026




Oh, and if Ukko Pekka Luukkonen has heard the BUF-NYR-WPG triumvirate trade chatter, he certainly didn’t show it. 



Win a damned faceoff. The Leafs led the period 13-7 at the dot and led to a lot of their puck possession.



Remember that whole thing about the Leafs having a plodding defense and that the Sabres should go up the ice vertically against them? Yeah they didn’t really, and the one time they did they scored. 



The Sabres jumped on the Leafs to start, leading 7-2 on shots, but the period ended 15-8 to Toronto. 



The Leafs got lucky with the the refs (hmmm) when they got an undeserving power play to close out the period after their own player high-sticked his teammate. The Leafs fifth-ranked power play ended the period 1 of 2 with a dozen second left in the man advantage. 




Sam Carrick gets a two-minute penalty for having OEL high stick his own teammate pic.twitter.com/PdvV1cdkjn— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 15, 2026




Second Period – Drought-era Sabres



The Sabres killed of the overlapping power play before Quinn continued his Leaf ownage, scoring his ninth goal in 15 games against Toronto, displaying his patience before McCabe bit and the Sabres forward blasted home over Bobrovsky’s shoulder. 



He almost had a hattie a few minutes later when he waltzed through a static D but Bob refused to be embarrassed again. 




Jack Quinn's 2nd goal of the game, 2-2 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/zdINNj5aRq— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Olen Zellweger decided not only was he going to replace Bowen Byram in the Sabres lineup, but he was going to take a further step and fill Rasmus Dahlin’s sizeable skates. He’s been very visible the last few games and was good again tonight. 



A full session of turnover-filled hockey in the neutral zone then ensued. As the Sabres then got lulled to sleep, Tavares won a board battle in the middle of the period, fed Marchenko and he beat UPL glove side for his second of the game to make it 3-2. 



Quinn hit the post and was active throughout the period again, and when Tage Thompson drew a penalty, Quinn even dropped the gloves against faux hard man Stecher. While he didn’t land a punch, he did wrestle his man to the ice and both drew five for fighting which alas hurt the Sabres more with their in-form top scorer taken off the ice. 



Remember when Knies was traded to the Blue Jackets on the eve of the season and then promptly scored twice against the Sabres on debut? Well the piece that went the other way was Marchenko and then with three minutes left Doan lost him in the blue paint he promptly got his hattrick to make it 4-2. 



With just under two to play Rielly went off for hooking, but Benson took an immature penalty holding on to Sissons’s stick. But unlike that night when the Habs were not punished for that, Benson took a penalty and the power play was wasted. 



Once again the Sabres were going to a third period having spotted their opponent a two-goal lead, despite having outshot the Leafs 13-11 in the period. 



Third Period – Division-winning Sabres



The Sabres have eight third period goals and it has been their best period by far. This one started with the same verve too with Buffalo humming around Bob’s net. 



Paul tripped Josh Norris into Tavares, sending the Leafs forward down the tunnel to the dressing room. 



Tonight though, while Quinn was feeling it, who from the Sabres would step up and get a goal to add some pressure on the home side? Last season it was the defense, and once again tonight it was the dmen again. 



Well, Quinn found Dennis Gilbert at the blue line halfway through the period and the dman fired home over Bob’s pad to make it 4-3. That gave Quinn a very well-deserved Gordie Howe hattrick. Congrats to Buffalo boy and the much-loved Gibby for his first Sabres goal!




Dennis Gilbert gets on the board to make it 4-3 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/M9CbWYHlaX— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Toronto were rocking on their heels and just two minutes later, Mattias Samuelsson joined the rush, took a feed from Tage and roofed a shot over Bob to make it 4-4 and the Scotiabank Arena was hushed. At that point the Sabres were outshooting the Leafs 10-1!




Mattias Samuelsson gets involved and ties the game, 4-4 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/xcVa9T0p9Y— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Toronto belatedly woke up after that, but the rest of regulation time elapsed with little drama, 4-4 and advantage Sabres 11-4 for the period on shots. 



Overtime – He’s Got The Power!



Unlike the OT in Quebec two nights ago when the Sabres barely had a sniff of the puck for five minutes, this one was more end-to-end. 



Benson had the puck on a three-on-one and then whiffed on his pass. Then Norris got clattered in the Leafs defensive zone and Power wisely held on to the puck to allow the forward to hobble off the ice. They went straight up the guy after that with Östlund feeding up Power who then fired off a howitzer to beat Bobrovsky for another OT winner!




Owen Power overtime winner, 5-4 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/luzb3aqI1C— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Make that three straight goals scored by defensemen tonight when the forwards minus Quinn were all sputtering. 



At The Horn



The Sabres simply cannot keep spotting teams leads going into the third period and assuming they can just reel them back in, especially against offensively endowed teams like the Leafs and and even more so when they are still without captain Rasmus Dahlin. 



Luukkonen wasn’t bad tonight, but as he has so often this season, he saved shots he shouldn’t have, and was beaten by shots he should have saved, ending the night on a deficit of -1.03 once again in the Goals Saved Above Average.

stories.title: Game #8 Preview & Open Thread: Sabres at Maple Leafs
stories.summary:
Buffalo renews rivalry with Toronto



Buffalo Sabres (3-3-1) at Toronto Maple Leafs (3-3-1)



Puck Drop: 7 p.m. ET | Scotiabank Arena, Toronto



TV: MSG-B, TSN4, DAZN, ESPN+, Fubo



Radio: WGR 550, Sirius XM (app)



Know Your Opponent



Toronto Maple Leafs



Record: 3-3-1 | 7 PTS



Last Game: 5-4 loss at Utah



Division Ranking: 6th



PP: 5th, 29.2% [Sabres: 30th, 11.1%]



PK: 1st, 95.8% [Sabres: 30th, 60.9%]



Season Series: Sabres 3-0-1 vs. Maple Leafs in 2025-26 season



What to Watch



1. Zellweger shining in Dahlin’s absence



Olen Zellweger already had big shoes to fill when he was acquired from Anaheim this offseason, and when Sabres captain Rasmus Dahlin went down with an injury in Monday’s win over the Panthers, it forced the 23-year-old into an even bigger role.



Fortunately for Buffalo, he’s certainly looked the part so far.



Zellweger had two goals and finished with a career-high 25:49 of ice time in Tuesday’s shootout loss in Montreal, and led Sabres skaters in shots on goal for the second consecutive game. With Dahlin out again against the Maple Leafs, another standout performance from Zellweger could go a long way toward securing two points in a divisional matchup.



2. Luukkonen finding his game?



Sabres coach Lindy Ruff kept it suffice on Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen’s performance following Tuesday’s game: “Our goalie got us a point.”



Luukkonen stopped 35-of-38 shots against the Canadiens, including a crucial late save with 3 seconds remaining in regulation that secured the Sabres a point. He also finished with a positive goals saved above expected for the second consecutive game, according to Hockeystats.com, following a strong relief appearance against Florida. Despite an abnormally poor showing in the shootout, it seemed like the Finn was finally beginning to get into a rhythm in the crease.



The Sabres will look to Luukkonen again to start on Thursday, but he faces a bogey team in the Maple Leafs. The 27-year-old is 0-5-2 in eight appearances against Toronto in his career.



3. Early elation to frustration



The Sabres were a remarkable 36-6-2 when scoring first last season, a conversion rate that played a major factor in sending the franchise back to the playoffs, but it’s been tough sledding in that category to start this campaign.



Buffalo is 1-2-1 this season when tallying the first goal, a worrying trend albeit one with a small sample size. On top of that, in all four games the Sabres have scored first, they have failed to get the next goal and been outscored 7-3 in the second period.



Should the Sabres score first for the fifth time this season against Toronto, following up on that early momentum would be a welcome sight.



Injury Notes



In addition to being without Dahlin on Thursday, the Sabres will also be down Tyson Kozak, who is dealing with an upper-body injury. Ruff said Wednesday that goalie Alex Lyon suffered a setback in his recovery from a shoulder injury, meaning he’ll be off the ice for a few days after returning to practice last week.



Toronto will be without defenseman Chris Tanev, who is week-to-week with an upper-body injury suffered in the Maple Leafs’ win over Colorado on Sunday.

stories.title: Sabres escape Montreal with a point, lose 4-3 in shootout
stories.summary:
Score: Buffalo Sabres 3, Montreal Canadiens 4 (SO)



Shots: Buffalo 17, Montreal 38



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Zellweger (1) (Samuelsson, Malenstyn); Norris (1) (Gilbert, Malenstyn); Zellweger (2) (Benson, Samuelsson)



Montreal Canadiens Goals: Lane Hutson (1) (Slafkovský, Caufield); Caufield (3) (Slafkovský, N. Suzuki); Anderson (2) (Huston, Bolduc)



SO Goals



Sabres: Thompson



Montreal: Caufield; Texier; Bolduc



Summary



The Buffalo Sabres (3-3-1), facing some adversity without Captain Rasmus Dahlin dressed, dropped Tuesday night’s game to the Montreal Canadiens (3-2-1) by a score of 4-3 in a shootout. Sabres goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen stops 35 of 38 shots in the loss, including a couple big saves at the end to help secure the Sabres a point. 



A Stop and Go First



It was a sluggish start for both sides in the game, as multiple whistles in the first few minutes prevented either team from finding consistent footing. 



This actually ended up to the Sabres benefit early on.



Just over two minutes into the game, defenseman Olen Zellweger, who was thrust into a bigger role with Dahlin out of the lineup, ripped a shot from the point. Thanks to a friendly bounce off the skate of a Canadiens’ defender in front, this otherwise innocuous shot would give the Sabres a nice early 1-0 lead. 



The flurry of stoppages continued even after the Sabres got their early lead, including one where linesman Ryan Daisy was accidentally hit by Jiri Kulich off a faceoff scrum, leading to Daisy having to be helped off the ice. The game continued with just three officials.



The Sabres went without a shot on goal after their goal until a Too Many Men penalty led to a Sabres power play, and while they did not score, they managed four shots on goal within that two minute span and kept the zone pressure for the entirety of the man advantage. Montreal did not manage one clear, as Benson and Ostlund in particular hounded the Montreal penalty kill unit. While none of the shots were incredibly high danger, it was another encouraging sign for the Sabres power play. Notably with Dahlin out, Power was manning the point alone in his stead. 



Still with their 1-0 lead, the Canadiens found themselves with a golden opportunity. Josh Norris made an ill-advised pass that led to a two-on-zero rush. With a golden chance, Josh Anderson took a cross ice feed and buried it right into the net of Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen’s glove. It was an amazing save by Luukkonen to keep the Sabres lead intact. 



The lead would not last for much longer though, back to back penalties by Zellweger and Louis Crevier would give Montreal a 5 on 3 power play. While the Sabres did a nice job for the first portion, Lane Hutson would make them pay, tying the game 1-1 on a shot from the point. 



Thankfully for the Sabres, they were able to kill enough of the second penalty to whittle it down to 18 seconds left when Montreal would take a penalty of their own, this time a hold. The ensuing Sabres power play was not as effective as the first one, as they struggled to keep zone pressure. The rest of the period remained uneventful, as the Sabres and Habs entered the first period with the score at 1-1. Montreal did have the shot edge in the period, 11-7. 



Uneventful and Opportunistic



The second period started in a sluggish fashion too, but unlike the first period, this was to the Sabres’ disadvantage. Montreal had a good amount of early pressure, which led to the Krebs-Thompson-Doan line being out there for an extended shift. As they tried to push back on offense, they got caught up ice and couldn’t get back, giving Montreal a 4-on-2 rush, leading to the puck finding the stick of Cole Caufield, who made no mistake, blowing a one-timer by Luukkonen to give them a 2-1 lead just two minutes into the period. 



The Sabres continued in the early part of the second period being unable to sustain anything of note. This was not for lack of chances to drive play though, as they found themselves with two early power plays, one before the Caufield goal, and one a few minutes after. Despite the hope the first one gave, the ensuing three opportunities left a lot to be desired. 



What the power play for the Sabres did accomplish, however, was completely stifling momentum for both teams. After that power play, both teams went about 10 minutes recording one shot each. Montreal would get a power play of their own with five minutes remaining in the period, once again bringing the Sabres a challenge on the penalty kill. 



While the Sabres killed that penalty, they could not escape the period down a goal. With under a minute to go, Ryan McLeod failed to clear the puck from the defensive zone, leading to sustained pressure. Unfortunately for McLeod, the puck found the stick of the most dangerous Canadien, Lane Hutson, who drew the attention of every Sabres defender. Hutson slid the puck over to a completely uncovered Anderson, who made no mistake burying a one-timer top shelf past Luukkonen to give the Canadiens a 3-1 lead going into the third period.



The Sabres mustered just two shots in the period, despite even having two opportunities with the man advantage. The Canadiens, despite a 10 minute stretch where they recorded two shots, ended with 11 in the period. The Sabres on the season have been outscored 13-4 in the second period of games so far this season. 



In his post game press conference, Sabres coach Lindy Ruff said the second period against the Canadiens “may have been one of our worst periods in a long time.”



Live with the bounces



The Sabres must have gotten a message heading into the third because they came out with a different pace than they had the first two periods. Just four minutes into the period, Norris put in some good work to win a wall battle, skated to the point, and let a shot go that bounced off a defender before going in the net, cutting the lead to 3-2. It was the first goal of the season for Norris, whose struggles have been one of the biggest talking points of the season for the Sabres so far, but he put in some nice work on that shift to get rewarded with the bounce.



The bounces would continue just a few minutes later, with Olen Zellweger benefitting from a bounce once again. Very similar to the first two Sabres goals, Zellweger let a point shot go that deflected off a defender and past Montreal goalie Jacob Fowler again, tying the game at three, just one minute after Norris scored to cut the lead to one. 



Montreal would respond with a flurry of chances following the tying goal, peppering Luukkonen with shots and while none of them were incredibly high danger, he still faced a ton of action with a flurry of shots. 



After that flurry, both teams seemed content to get a point in overtime. The only real chance until the final few seconds of the game was a Sabres 2-on-1 at the end of a shift that led to Fowler making the save on Josh Doan. 



While the game did indeed go to an extra frame, catastrophe almost struck in the twilight of regulation. Montreal had possession with just under 10 seconds left in the period, and a defensive miscue led to Phillip Danault being all alone in front with the puck off a feed from the wall. Danault put a deflection on Luukkonen, who stood firm, making the initial save and an ensuing rebound save to ensure his team would at least gain one point in the standings. 



Overtime Possessed



Montreal completely dominated possession in the overtime period, putting up five shots in the frame to the Sabres zero. No shots, however, did not mean the Sabres went without chances to win it. 



A Josh Doan that was broken up before he could get a shot off, and actually ended the frame on a 30 second power play from a holding penalty on Juraj Slafkovsky. Some questionable antics from Jake Evans, grabbing the sticks of both Benson and Quinn while lying on the puck on the ice helped kill off that penalty. The Sabres got a couple nice looks at the end of the frame but couldn’t get a puck on Fowler. The game would then go to everyone’s favorite party game…



The Shootout



The Canadiens seemingly had something on Luukkonen, as they scored on all three attempts in the shootout and all attacked from the same angle. Both Caufield and Texier skated right to left and beat Luukkonen clean with a wrister, while Bolduc skated the same direction and beat him through the 5-hole on a deke. The Sabres went 5-1 in games that went to a shootout last season, an area that Luukkonen was great in. The Sabres coaching staff will have some work to do figuring out how to help Luukkonen so this doesn’t continue to happen.



Wrap Up



The Sabres, while they of course would have wanted two, have to feel pretty good escaping this game with a point. They were outplayed for a majority of the game and struggled to generate any offense, despite even having five power play opportunities in the game. All three Sabre goals came off point shot deflections, meaning the result could have been much worse, especially considering they were on the wrong end of a back to back without their best player.



While he let in three goals, Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen is the main reason the Sabres escaped even with one point. Stopping 35 of 38 shots on a night where the team in front of him was really struggling to generate offense is exactly what the Sabres needed to see from their goalie. 



Although he finished with negative goals saved above expected, he didn’t have much of a chance on any of the three that went in, and he made plenty of big time saves to keep the Sabres in the game when they were down and to get the game to overtime once it was tied.



With the Sabres down their captain, they needed a few members of their defense corps to step up. Power and Samuelsson were their normal steady self, but the team had to be incredibly encouraged by Olen Zellweger’s performance in this game. Leaving the two goals aside, he logged over 25 minutes of ice time, only trailing Power and Samuelsson among the defensemen, and has potentially found himself in the circle of trust. If Zellweger can be this kind of player for the Sabres, they will miss Bowen Byram less and less as the season goes on. 



What’s Next



The Sabres will travel to Toronto on Thursday for a showdown with the revamped Maple Leafs. It is unknown to this point if Dahlin will be back in the lineup, but he has not yet been ruled out for the game.

Buffalo Returns to Montreal for First Meeting Since Playoff Elimination



Know Your Opponent

Season Series: First meeting of 2026-27



What to Watch



1. Back to the Scene of the Crime



The Buffalo Sabres return to Montreal tonight for the first time since their season ended in Game 7 of the second round of the Stanley Cup Playoffs. Alex Newhook’s overtime winner sent the Canadiens to the Eastern Conference Final and left Buffalo wondering what could have been. Now, less than five months later, the two Atlantic Division rivals meet again. While the stakes aren’t nearly as high this time around, there should still be some extra motivation for the Sabres. Buffalo enters tonight’s contest coming off a much-needed 5-3 victory over Florida on Monday afternoon. After Dallas shut them out and Utah allowed only one goal, the Sabres finally got their offense going. Montreal has also had an inconsistent start to the season, sitting at 2-2-1 after Saturday’s shootout win over Detroit. The Canadiens have plenty of offensive talent, but have struggled to put together complete performances. With Buffalo playing the second half of a back-to-back, a strong start will be important.



2. No Dahlin, No Problem?



The biggest storyline heading into tonight is Rasmus Dahlin’s absence. The Sabres captain left Monday’s game against Florida with an upper-body injury and did not travel with the team to Montreal. Dahlin is considered day-to-day, but losing him creates a significant problem for Buffalo. He leads the team’s defense, runs the power play, and plays in nearly every serious situation. Owen Power will need to take on a bigger role. Power has been one of Buffalo’s better starters this season, recording seven points in six games. His offensive production has been encouraging, but tonight will also test his ability to handle more defensive responsibility. Mattias Samuelsson will also be relied on heavily, while Dennis Gilbert has been recalled from Rochester after Matt Grzelcyk was placed on injured reserve. Montreal’s top line of Cole Caufield, Nick Suzuki and Juraj Slafkovsky will present a difficult matchup, particularly without Buffalo’s best defenseman.



3. Special Teams Remain a Problem



Buffalo finally got its power play going against Florida, scoring twice on five opportunities. Dahlin and Noah Östlund each converted with the man advantage, giving the Sabres three power-play goals over their last two games. Unfortunately, the penalty kill remains a disaster. The Panthers entered Monday’s contest with one of the league’s worst power plays and still managed to score twice on four opportunities. Buffalo’s penalty killing percentage has fallen to just 60%, ranking near the bottom of the NHL. Montreal hasn’t been much better on the power play, converting just one of its first 17 opportunities this season. Something has to give tonight. The Canadiens have enough talent in Suzuki, Caufield, and Lane Hutson to make Buffalo pay if the Sabres keep allowing cross-ice passes and quality scoring chances. With Dahlin out, the Sabres will also need someone to quarterback the top power-play unit. Power would be the obvious candidate, and it will be interesting to see how Lindy Ruff adjusts.



4. Can the Sabres Find Some Consistency?



Goaltending is another concern. Colten Ellis was pulled Monday after allowing two goals on nine shots, leaving Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen to finish the game. Luukkonen made 13 saves in relief and is expected to get the start tonight. Monday’s win over Florida was encouraging, but the Sabres still have plenty to clean up. Buffalo has alternated between looking like the team that won the Atlantic Division last season and the team that spent more than a decade missing the playoffs. Against Dallas and Utah, the Sabres struggled to generate consistent offensive pressure. Against Florida, they moved their feet, attacked the middle of the ice, and created opportunities around the net. Tage Thompson has been Buffalo’s most consistent offensive threat, with four goals and seven points in six games. The Sabres need their other forwards to continue contributing. Josh Doan and Ryan McLeod both scored their first goals of the season Monday, while Östlund continues to establish himself as an important part of the lineup. The Sabres don’t need their goalie to steal every game, but they do need more dependable performances if they want to compete with the better teams in the Atlantic Division.

Final Thoughts



It’s hard to overstate the importance of a mid-October game, but tonight gives Buffalo a chance to build momentum. The Sabres have a difficult stretch of divisional games ahead, including Thursday’s matchup in Toronto and another meeting with Montreal on Saturday. Getting points against Atlantic Division opponents will be critical if Buffalo hopes to repeat last season’s success. Playing without Dahlin makes things more difficult, but it is also a chance to see whether the Sabres have enough depth to overcome injuries to key players. Buffalo showed against Florida that it can generate offense throughout the lineup. Now it needs to do so consistently while playing a more responsible defensive game. A win tonight would move the Sabres above .500 for the first time since beating Minnesota last week.

Buffalo’s Power Play Coming Around as the PK Sinks Further



Score: Buffalo Sabres 5-3 Florida PanthersShots: BUF 32-23 FLA



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Doan 1st (Krebs) Dahlin 2nd PPG (Quinn, Thompson) McLeod 1st (Zellweger, Power) Ostlund 2nd PPG (Benson, Quinn) Thompson 4th (Power, Krebs)Florida Panthers Goals: Lundell 1st ( Ekblad, Vilmanis) Reinhart 1st PPG (Jones, M. Tkachuk) Reinhart 2nd PPG (B. Tkachuk,  Jones)



Plus 1: Sabres Pounce Early 



The Sabres came out with some jam today, firing shots early and generating better scoring chances than we’ve seen recently. Buffalo registered the game’s first five shots, keeping Jacob Markstrom busy right from the get-go. Josh Doan had one of the better opportunities, backhanding a rebound on goal from about 12 feet out. No dice for the snakebitten and apparently ailing Josh.



Buffalo cashed in at the 5:58 mark, with the aforementioned Josh Doan finally breaking his personal goose egg on the season. On a rush, Josh worked a give-and-go with Peyton Krebs, dishing him the puck near center ice. Krebs returned the favor with a perfect pass, sending Doan skating into the Panthers’ zone before he fired it past Markstrom. That was a King Kong-sized monkey finally coming off Doan’s back. The Sabres were dominating the early action, outshooting Florida 8-1 at that point.



A little later, Josh Norris had a golden opportunity when he redirected a pass off the wall toward the net while all alone in front. This time, Markstrom came up big. That missed chance would prove costly. Shortly afterward, Colton Ellis made the initial stop for Buffalo but couldn’t corral the rebound. After a scramble for the puck, Anton Lundell’s backhand somehow squeaked between Ellis’s pads—a weakness that has shown up a few times already—and into the net to tie the game.



Thankfully, Buffalo wasted little time getting that goal back on the power play. Steady now, folks—it’s true! Rasmus Dahlin unleashed a blast that found the back of the net, with Jack Quinn and Tage Thompson picking up the assists. However, credit Noah Ostlund for making it happen in the first place. His stickhandling and patience in the corner helped create the opportunity that led to the goal.



The Sabres earned another man advantage late in the period, but this one was nowhere near as effective. After 20 minutes, Buffalo held an 11-7 edge in shots and a 2-1 lead on the scoreboard. The Sabres were bringing the energy early and often and played a good period of hockey.







Minus 1: PK Struggles and the Captain Goes Down



Though it wasn’t a bad period for Jacob Markstrom, Florida head coach Paul Maurice decided to make a change, inserting Akira Schmid in goal to start the second. Perhaps he was looking to shake things up a little, and for the most part, it seemed to work.



Olen Zellweger, who had been skating well all afternoon, helped generate several good chances for himself and his teammates during a strong shift early in the period. Buffalo earned another power play shortly after when Aaron Ekblad was called for interference on Josh Doan. The Sabres generated some decent looks but, once again, came away empty-handed.



Zellweger then found himself in the penalty box for tripping Sam Reinhart, and the former Sabre wasted little time making Buffalo pay. Reinhart scored on the power play for his first goal of the year — just as many predicted in the pregame. Once again, the puck squeaked between Colton Ellis’s pads before being tapped into the net. At this point, head coach Lindy Ruff decided to join in on the goalie-change festivities, pulling Ellis after he surrendered two goals on just nine shots. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen entered the game and was greeted by the boo birds from the KeyBank Center faithful. Buffalo has generally done a decent job of limiting opponents’ shots this season, but the goaltending simply hasn’t been there.



The Sabres responded with Ryan McLeod netting his first goal of the year. Toothless drove to the net, got around the defense, deked Schmid and tucked the puck home. Credit Owen Power and Zellweger for quickly transitioning the puck up ice and helping create the scoring opportunity. But the fans barely had time to settle back into their seats before gritty forward Beck Malenstyn, who had been having a solid shift, was whistled for holding. Former Sabre Sam Reinhart would strike again, burying his second power-play goal of the game. Buffalo’s penalty kill has been nearly as dreadful as it’s man advantage, and that’s saying something.



After two periods, the game was tied at three. However, the biggest concern had little to do with the scoreboard. Sabres captain Rasmus Dahlin was absent from the bench for some time before the team finally announced he had suffered an upper-body injury and would not return. Because apparently, this struggling team didn’t have enough problems already.



Plus 2: From Booooo to Luuuuuu



The third period opened cautiously, with both teams managing just one shot apiece through the first five minutes. Buffalo eventually put together a strong shift, capitalizing on a turnover behind the net and generating several chances around the Florida goal. The pressure paid off when Aaron Ekblad was called for holding Zach Benson, giving the Sabres a power play that would ultimately prove to be the difference in the game.



Buffalo’s man advantage showed some more life as Noah Ostlund scored his second goal of the season. Ostlund fended off a Panthers defender before swiping the puck past Schmid to give the Sabres some much-needed insurance. Benson deserved plenty of credit for the goal after a slick pass and some nifty stickhandling behind the net, while Jack Quinn picked up his second assist of the game.



Luukkonen then came up with a big stop on a Garnet Hathaway tip, along with several other tough saves after allowing a goal shortly after entering the game. Those saves proved crucial when Owen Power found Tage Thompson alone in the slot. TNT made no mistake, ripping a rocket past the Florida goaltender for his team-leading fourth goal of the season. Just like that, Buffalo had a two-goal cushion. Peyton Krebs also collected his second assist of the game on the play.



From there, the Sabres dug in and made Florida work for everything, with Luukkonen holding the fort behind them. UPL turned aside all nine shots he faced in the third period, delivering arguably his best performance in a single frame this season. That included surviving a late Florida power play with the Panthers pulling their goaltender for an extra attacker.



Buffalo bent but didn’t break, hanging on for a much-needed victory. The win stopped the bleeding and gave the Sabres a respectable 3-2 finish to their five-game homestand. After a frustrating stretch, these were two points Buffalo desperately needed.









Final Thoughts:



The Sabres needed this win in the worst way, and they delivered a strong effort overall. Buffalo overcame many of the same adversities that have plagued them through the first six games of the season. Tage Thompson, Jack Quinn and Peyton Krebs each finished with two points, while Josh Doan and Ryan McLeod finally scored their first goals of the season. I also thought Olen Zellweger had a terrific game, skating hard, moving quickly and making his presence felt all over the ice. Zach Benson stood out as well, bringing his usual energy and tenacity.



The loss of Rasmus Dahlin is a major blow, and as of now, there is no timetable for his return. Hopefully, Lindy Ruff will have some positive news to share soon. The Sabres can ill afford to be without their captain for an extended stretch.



Buffalo is right back at it tomorrow night when they visit the Montréal Canadiens at the Bell Centre. This will be the first meeting between the two teams since the Sabres fell to Montreal in Game 7 of the second round of last season’s playoffs. There should be no shortage of motivation for Buffalo in this one. Take note of the unusual 6:30 p.m. Eastern start time.

Quick Thoughts



Ruff Was Already Mad



Lindy Ruff was already displeased with this team’s effort two nights ago in the blanking against the Dallas Stars, can only imagine how livid he’s going to be after this one. Bag skates tomorrow for the whole team. 



Sam Carrick and Tyson Kozak made the lineup with Konsta Helenius and Jiri Kulich both benched, with Ruff saying – “If you want to stay in the lineup you have to play hard and you’ve got to be bringing something to the table every night.”



Power Play Off The Schneid



The Sabres were the last team in the league to score a power play goal, and that came from a nifty move from Tage Thompson charging in from the right. However, the team then proceeded to draw a blank in their remaining three opportunities to temper that relief. 



Penalty Kill Woes



Special teams continues to struggle in both facets, with the penalty kill. Tonight they gave up another couple of goals in five power plays, and have now conceded six times in sixteen opportunities, with that 62.5% penalty kill putting them in about 30th place in the league. 



At The Horn



The Mammoth are off to a good start but got hammered 6-1 in Boston two nights ago. They were back to their fine form tonight with the Sabres continuing to falter, no matter who is in net. There’s just no chemistry on this team right now, with wayward passes and missed shots continuing to be hallmarks of their play. 



Buffalo are yet to beat Utah in now five games played since the new team was formed, and were not even close today. They were outhustled, outplayed and indeed, outcoached. Yet there’s no time to sulk about this result for the Sabres with four division games coming up. If they keep up this mediocre level of play in those Atlantic games they run the risk of getting cut adrift very early in the season in what could again be a hotly competitive division race.
